boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Anklam entry (capitulation, 1 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian columns of the brothers General Bila I and Bila II at Anklam and Beker's dragoon brigade (Bodart's Becker) with General Boussard's brigade, from the French arrival before Anklam on the morning of 31 October, with the defence of the Peene bridge and the capture of Rittmeister Hiller's detachments, to the capitulation agreed that day and carried out on 1 November. The columns' marches to Anklam are context; the capitulation of Major Langwerth's baggage column, negotiated at Anklam, belongs to the Wolgast entry and is not counted here. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as the French dragoon brigade Becker, about 1,000 men, and side B (Prussian) as 2,200 Prussians, 1,100 infantry and 1,100 cavalry, under General v. Bila, who laid down their arms before it; the men became prisoners of war and the officers were released on parole. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner, the French letters and the 25th Bulletin give other figures (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french, side-a-strength). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 1/11. capitulation of Anklam'; 'before the French dragoon brigade Becker (about 1,000 men) 2,200 Prussians (1,100 infantry, 1,100 cavalry) under General v. Bila lay down their arms, after which the men became prisoners of war and the officers were released on their word of honour'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: two columns under two brothers met at Anklam. General Bila I had left Hanover on 20 October with the 1st battalion of the regiment vac. Grävenitz, the depots of the fusilier battalions Wedel and Kaiserlingk, a detachment of 120 horses of the Bailliodz cuirassiers and the Hildesheim and Hanover cash boxes and archive. At Anklam he found the grenadier battalion Sack, which had escorted the war chest there under Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz, and a company of the regiment Treuenfels from the escort of Major Langwerth's baggage, and ordered both to join his corps; his 120 Bailliodz horses were quartered at Görke, where the depot of the Leib-Kürassier regiment and a detachment of Hertzberg dragoons already stood. His brother, General Bila II, was expected with almost 1000 horses and filed through Anklam at daybreak on the 31st; on his march the cuirassiers of the regiment Quitzow and a troop of the Leib-Karabinier regiment had joined him (OCR passages). The general surrendered with 1100 infantry and 1073 horses.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 222, 225, 226 and 230, with the opening of Höpfner's account of Bila II's march, the cavalry that joined him and the end of p. 224 from the OCR. The columns were brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner does not say whether Rittmeister Hiller's detachments, captured outside the town (claim side-b-losses), are in his 1100 infantry and 1073 horses. English renderings (ours): 'meanwhile the minister Ingersleben received a letter from Colonel Scharnhorst which assumed that General Bila I had already withdrawn from Hanover'; 'this and the news, spreading ever further, of the dissolution of the Prussian army decided the general to set out from Hanover on 20 October with the 1st battalion of the regiment vac. Grävenitz, the depots of the fusilier battalions Wedel and Kaiserlingk, a detachment of 120 horses of the regiment of Bailliodz cuirassiers, the Hildesheim and Hanover cash boxes and the Hanover archive, and to take a northerly direction so as not to collide with the retreating army'; 'at Anklam General Bila I found the grenadier ba-' (OCR); 'ttalion Sack and a company of the regiment Treuenfels'; 'the grenadiers had marched off with Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz from Lindow on the 26th as escort of the war chest, and had stayed in Anklam to hold an urgently needed rest day, after the lieutenant colonel had carried out the embarkation of the war chest on the 29th'; 'the company of Treuenfels belonged to the escort of the baggage that had left Genthin under Major Langwerth'; 'he stayed in the town with the infantry; the 120 horses of Bailliodz were quartered at Görke, on the road to Demmin, where the depot of the Leib-Kürassier regiment and a detachment of Hertzberg dragoons under Lieutenant v. d. Gröben already stood'; 'was reported, and General Bila II was also to arrive with almost 1000 horses, a decision had to be taken on the further retreat. The Bila infantry was to be embarked at Pinnow, the baggage at Wolgast'; 'when General Bila I arrived at Anklam at 10 o'clock in the evening, he ordered that the grenadier battalion Sack and the company of Treuenfels should join his corps'; 'we left General Bila II' (OCR); 'before Strasburg the cuirassiers of the regiment Quitzow under Colonel Heiligenstädt, who had become separated from Colonel Schubärt, and further on a troop of the Leib-Karabinier regiment joined him' (OCR); '... to come to know the bad spirit bred in the troops by (misfor)tunes, hardships and want of every kind, General Bila set out again at midnight, and at daybreak on the 31st filed through Anklam, where he united by chance with his brother, the infantry general Bila I'; 'at daybreak General Bila II filed through Anklam and drew up beyond the town'; 'as there was added to this the fatigue of men and horses, the idea of not being able to live on the island of Usedom, and the request of the town of Anklam not to ruin it by a further defence of the Peene, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements at all to cross the Peene at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation, and surrendered to the enemy with 1100 men of infantry and 1073 horses on 1 November'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures. Lasalle wrote on 30 October, citing a postillon, of a corps outside Anklam of guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers and dragoons, with many infantry and above all baggage and no guns, put at 6,000 men. Beker wrote on 31 October of a corps of 2,000 men, and then of a column of 3,000 men, 1,000 to 1,200 of them cavalry, commanded by 2 generals; on 2 November, writing that the capture was larger than it had first seemed, he gave an aide-de-camp's count: besides the 2 generals, 1,200 and some mounted cavalry and more than 1,500 infantry, including 1 battalion of 700 grenadiers, with 1 flag and 4 horsed guns. Murat wrote on 1 November that the corps was 3,000 to 4,000 men, with guns, 2 generals, 2 cavalry regiments and a strong detachment of a 3rd, and 1,400 or 1,500 horses to be received. The 25th Bulletin gives 4,000 prisoners of war, and Mathieu Dumas, as Höpfner quotes him, about four thousand, among them the hussars of the King's guard.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images, with Dumas from Höpfner's footnote on the page image of p. 226; not reconciled with each other or with Höpfner's and Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). The column was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. Beker also wrote that the number of officers far exceeded that of the soldiers, which is kept as printed. English renderings (ours): Lasalle, 'General Lasalle to the Grand Duke of Berg. Falkenwald, 30 October 1806, 7 o'clock in the evening'; 'a postillon coming back from Anklam, who left it yesterday at 5 o'clock in the evening, says that outside the gate there are many infantry, cavalry and above all baggage, that their camp stretches half a league on this side, towards Uckermünde. There are no guns. Guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers, dragoons, remnants of the Prussian army, make up this corps. The name of its commander is not known. The bridge of Anklam is cut on the side of Sweden. This corps is put at 6,000 men; it comes from Mecklenburg and detachments of it arrive every day'; Beker, 'General Beker to the Grand Duke of Berg. Anklam, 31 October 1806'; 'having observed with General Boussard during the day a corps of 2,000 men who had taken refuge in Pomerania, having had'; 'everything that remained on the left bank of the river charged, and taken in various attacks more than 300 cavalry and as many infantry, I have succeeded, by multiplying my demonstrations and summoning the general to give himself up as a prisoner, in forcing him to accept the capitulation that has been customary in such circumstances'; 'at this moment 2 officers sent by General Bila are leaving here, with whom I have treated on the conditions prescribed by General Belliard. Thus tomorrow morning this column, 3,000 men strong, of whom 1,000 to 1,200 cavalry, and commanded by 2 generals, will lay down its arms and be directed on Friedland, where Your Highness will give it a destination, allowing the officers to retire to their homes with their baggage, to which they are infinitely attached'; 'General Beker to General Belliard. Friedland, 2 November 1806'; 'it is not without trouble that I have managed to drive the column out of Pomerania to take it to Potsdam; the capture being larger than it seemed at first, it is extremely difficult to keep everyone in hand and to lead them through a country whose resources are exhausted'; 'to have an exact view of all that makes up the column, I have commissioned an aide-de-camp to count the men'; 'and the horses captured until I can gather all the materials that must serve to draw up a return'; 'according to the count made by this officer, there are, besides the 2 generals, 1,200 and some mounted cavalry and more than 1,500 infantry, of whom 1 battalion of 700 grenadiers, 1 flag and 4 horsed guns'; 'the number of officers far exceeds that of the soldiers, and of these several have stayed behind to wait for the equipages they had sent to the island of Usedom, on whose recovery they fix their whole attention'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 1 November 1806, half past 4 in the morning'; 'I hasten to announce to Your Majesty that the whole corps which I had been told had embarked at Anklam is in the power of your troops. General Bila, who commands it, has surrendered to General Beker, whom I am charging to take this corps to Spandau with General Boussart's dragoon brigade'; 'the corps that has capitulated is 3,000 to 4,000 men strong; there are guns and 2 generals, 2 regiments of cavalry and a strong detachment of a 3rd. To keep 1,400 or 1,500 horses that we shall receive, I am ordering General Beker to confine himself to disarming the cavalry and to take these regiments mounted as far as Potsdam, where they will hand over their horses to General Bourcier'; the Bulletin, '25th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 2 November 1806'; 'the result of this capitulation was 4,000 prisoners of war. The officers are sent home on parole and the soldiers are taken to France. Among these prisoners is the regiment of hussars of the King's guard, which, after the Seven Years' War, had received from the Empress Catherine, in token of their good conduct, pelisses of tiger skin'; Dumas, 'the report of the French on the events at Anklam runs as follows, after Matthieu Dumas'; 'General Becker reached Bila's column on the plain in front of the little town of Anclam; he charged it at the head of General Broussart's dragoon brigade, broke the Prussian cavalry and infantry, threw them back into the town, entered it pell-mell with the enemy, and forced General Bila to capitulate. About four thousand prisoners, among whom were the hussars of the King's guard, fell into his hands'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives the dragoon brigade Becker, about 1,000 men. Höpfner: the dragoon brigade Becker, which had already gone ahead to Pasewalk, was at once set moving from there on Anklam (OCR passage), and the French had no guns. Beker wrote that he had observed the corps during the day with General Boussard; that Boussard's brigade was extremely reduced and would barely suffice to escort the column, his own regiments being almost melted away; and he asked for 1 regiment of the division to hold Anklam. Murat wrote that he was sending Beker a gun to knock down the drawbridge, and Belliard that detachments Beker had left behind had set out the evening before to join him with a gun Belliard was sending (OCR passage). The 25th Bulletin has Beker charge with General Boussart's dragoon brigade. No passage read gives a headcount for side A.
claims.rationale: Bodart, Höpfner and the French letters, read from the page images, with the OCR passages marked. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'he therefore hurried with the dragoon division Grouchy and the infantry division Süchet on the ... from Löcknitz to Pasewalk, from where the dragoon brigade Becker, which had already gone ahead there, was at once set in motion towards Anklam' (OCR); 'at this moment, however, the enemy also appeared before Anklam, and Captain Poyda with the rear guard left behind in the town barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge'; 'it was the dragoon brigade Becker that appeared before the two generals Bila. As the French had no'; 'guns with them, Captain Poyda defended the Peene bridge steadfastly, while General Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow'; Beker, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading and the corps observed; 'as General Boussard's brigade is extremely reduced, it will barely suffice for the escort of this column, and I shall have to leave Anklam, unless Your Highness thinks fit to send me 1 regiment of the division to hold the only point on which the fugitives of the army are retreating'; 'if I am not reinforced by a regiment, since mine are almost melted away'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. claims.value: Höpfner: General Bila I, who reached Anklam at 10 in the evening, had the cash boxes and archives he had brought shipped to Usedom in the night before the 31st. On the morning of the 31st, with news of the enemy's approach growing, he had the troops fall in and sent the baggage to Pinnow to be ferried over before them; Major Nostitz went ahead to arrange the ferries, and the general left his brother to cross at Wolgast. He left Anklam at 7 in the morning and only then sent an orderly to Rittmeister Hiller at Görke to march through Anklam. As the enemy appeared, Captain Poyda with the rear guard barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge, and he held it until 5 in the evening while Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow, meaning to march off to Pinnow in the night. When Captain Zimietzki's grenadier company relieved Poyda, its captain accepted a parlementaire and sent him to the general. Despairing of escape, though his brother had fully prepared him for Stettin's fall, and weighing the fatigue of men and horses, the idea that they could not live on Usedom and the town's request not to be ruined by a further defence, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements to cross at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation. Höpfner judges that it differed little from Pasewalk: the infantry had only 1½ miles to march to the Pinnow ferry and the cavalry 2½ to Lassahn and 3 to Wolgast, and the town's request made no sense.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 225-227 and 230. Höpfner does not name his sources for this passage. English renderings (ours): 'when General Bila I arrived at Anklam at 10 o'clock in the evening, he ordered that the grenadier battalion Sack and the company of Treuenfels should join his corps'; 'General Bila I had the cash boxes and archives he had brought embarked for Usedom that same night before the 31st under the lead of Captain Heyden, to go to Kolberg or Danzig'; 'after the union of the two generals Bila had thus taken place, and the news of the enemy's approach had increased, General Bila I had the troops present in Anklam fall in on the morning of the 31st, but sent the baggage off to Pinnow, so that it would be across before the troops arrived'; 'Major Nostitz of vac. Grävenitz went ahead to set up the ferrying. The general left it to his brother to cross the Peene at Wolgast and to send an officer ahead there as well'; 'at 7 o'clock in the morning General Bila I left Anklam and only now sent an orderly to Rittmeister Hiller at Görke with the order to march through Anklam'; 'at this moment, however, the enemy also appeared before Anklam, and Captain Poyda with the rear guard left behind in the town barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge'; 'it was the dragoon brigade Becker that appeared before the two generals Bila. As the French had no'; 'guns with them, Captain Poyda defended the Peene bridge steadfastly, while General Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow'; 'the general intended to march off to Pinnow in the night, and would probably have carried out this intention undisturbed, had misfortune not brought him a parlementaire'; 'until 5 o'clock in the evening Captain Poyda had held his ground at the Peene bridge, when he was relieved there by the grenadier company of Captain Zimietzki'; as in claim side-a-command for the parlementaire; 'although the general had been fully prepared for this event by his brother, he nevertheless despaired of escaping with his troops, as the French could always forestall him again from Stettin'; 'as there was added to this the fatigue of men and horses, the idea of not being able to live on the island of Usedom, and the request of the town of Anklam not to ruin it by a further defence of the Peene, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements at all to cross the Peene at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation, and surrendered to the enemy with 1100 men of infantry and 1073 horses on 1 November'; 'this capitulation differs little from the one at Pasewalk. claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Anklam on 1 November: 2,200 Prussians under General v. Bila laid down their arms before the dragoon brigade Becker; the men became prisoners of war and the officers were released on parole. Höpfner: the general accepted the capitulation and surrendered with 1100 infantry and 1073 horses on 1 November. Beker wrote on 31 October that the column would lay down its arms the next morning; Murat, on 1 November, that Bila had surrendered to Beker; the 25th Bulletin, that Beker forced the column to capitulate, the officers being sent home on parole and the soldiers taken to France.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the French documents, read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. The capitulation was agreed on 31 October and the arms laid down on 1 November (Beker, Höpfner). Belliard had told Beker to make no more written capitulations, and no text of this one was read. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'as there was added to this the fatigue of men and horses, the idea of not being able to live on the island of Usedom, and the request of the town of Anklam not to ruin it by a further defence of the Peene, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements at all to cross the Peene at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation, and surrendered to the enemy with 1100 men of infantry and 1073 horses on 1 November'; Beker, 'General Beker to the Grand Duke of Berg. Anklam, 31 October 1806'; 'at this moment 2 officers sent by General Bila are leaving here, with whom I have treated on the conditions prescribed by General Belliard. Thus tomorrow morning this column, 3,000 men strong, of whom 1,000 to 1,200 cavalry, and commanded by 2 generals, will lay down its arms and be directed on Friedland, where Your Highness will give it a destination, allowing the officers to retire to their homes with their baggage, to which they are infinitely attached'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 1 November 1806, half past 4 in the morning'; 'I hasten to announce to Your Majesty that the whole corps which I had been told had embarked at Anklam is in the power of your troops. General Bila, who commands it, has surrendered to General Beker, whom I am charging to take this corps to Spandau with General Boussart's dragoon brigade'; the Bulletin, '25th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 2 November 1806'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg had his headquarters on the 31st at Friedland. His dispositions made, he ordered the attack on the column of the Prussian general Bila, which General Beker charged, on the plain in front of the little town of Anklam, with General Boussart's dragoon brigade. Everything was broken, cavalry and infantry, and General Beker entered the town with the enemy, whom he forced to capitulate'; 'the result of this capitulation was 4,000 prisoners of war. The officers are sent home on parole and the soldiers are taken to France. Among these prisoners is the regiment of hussars of the King's guard, which, after the Seven Years' War, had received from the Empress Catherine, in token of their good conduct, pelisses of tiger skin'.

Höpfner: the Peene bridge at Anklam could be drawn up; Bila I's infantry stood behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow, and Stolpe lay upstream; the baggage crossed the Peene onto Swedish territory; the infantry had 1½ miles to march to the Pinnow ferry and the cavalry 2½ to Lassahn and 3 to Wolgast, and Görke lay on the road to Demmin. Lasalle wrote, citing a postillon, that the corps' camp stretched half a league towards Uckermünde, and that the bridge of Anklam was cut on the side of Sweden; Beker, halted at Cosenow, wrote that the fog increased the darkness and the town was closed (OCR passage); Murat, that the rest of the enemy corps had crossed the Peene in the night and raised the drawbridge; the Bulletin speaks of a plain in front of the little town. Foucart's note puts Anklam 22 km from Friedland.
claims.rationale: Location and ground as described, read from the page images, with Beker's closed town from the OCR; no plan of Anklam was inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, Pomerania, on the Peene, 75 km north-west of Stettin)'; Höpfner, 'at this moment, however, the enemy also appeared before Anklam, and Captain Poyda with the rear guard left behind in the town barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge'; 'it was the dragoon brigade Becker that appeared before the two generals Bila. As the French had no'; 'guns with them, Captain Poyda defended the Peene bridge steadfastly, while General Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow'; as in claim side-a-command for Stolpe; 'the baggage column went over the Peene onto Swedish territory and formed a wagon laager, to continue the march from it'; as in claims side-b-command for the distances and side-b-strength for Görke; Lasalle, 'General Lasalle to the Grand Duke of Berg. Falkenwald, 30 October 1806, 7 o'clock in the evening'; 'a postillon coming back from Anklam, who left it yesterday at 5 o'clock in the evening, says that outside the gate there are many infantry, cavalry and above all baggage, that their camp stretches half a league on this side, towards Uckermünde. There are no guns. Guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers, dragoons, remnants of the Prussian army, make up this corps. The name of its commander is not known. The bridge of Anklam is cut on the side of Sweden. This corps is put at 6,000 men; it comes from Mecklenburg and detachments of it arrive every day'; Beker, as in claim side-a-command (OCR); Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 31 October 1806, 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'I had the honour to announce to you this morning that I was marching on Friedland, and that I would have summoned by General'; 'Beker the enemy corps that was at Anklam, while General Lasalle would push before him everything on the road from Stettin to Anklam, making for Stretense'; 'General Beker reports to me that he has indeed carried out my order, but that he has taken prisoner only the tail of this corps, the rest having crossed the Peene in the night and raised the drawbridge on him. 400 men have fallen into his power, of whom 260 mounted cuirassiers'; the Bulletin, '25th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 2 November 1806'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg had his headquarters on the 31st at Friedland. His dispositions made, he ordered the attack on the column of the Prussian general Bila, which General Beker charged, on the plain in front of the little town of Anklam, with General Boussart's dragoon brigade. Everything was broken, cavalry and infantry, and General Beker entered the town with the enemy, whom he forced to capitulate'; Foucart's note, '2. From Cosenow to Friedland by Dargibell, 20 km; from Friedland to Anklam, 22 km'.

claims.value: Lasalle wrote on 30 October, citing a postillon who had left Anklam the previous evening, of a corps of guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers and dragoons, with many infantry and much baggage and no guns, its commander unknown, put at 6,000 men, with detachments arriving every day. Beker approached Anklam on the evening of the 30th to reconnoitre the bivouac fires on the Stettin road, found the point guarded by a picket of hussars backed by infantry, and heard from peasants and a postillon that the town was crowded with fugitives from every regiment; he would summon the officer commanding the troops at daybreak, who, he wrote, did not know how near the French were or where to retreat, since Beker was certain that the Swedes refused to receive them in Pomerania, except their baggage (OCR passages). On 31 October Beker wrote that he was certain Blücher had recrossed the Oder 5 days before. After the capitulation an order from Friedland for chef d'escadron Boyer found it astonishing that no one could yet say whether the corps that had capitulated belonged to Blücher's or Hohenlohe's column (OCR passage).

There are no guns. Guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers, dragoons, remnants of the Prussian army, make up this corps. The name of its commander is not known. The bridge of Anklam is cut on the side of Sweden. This corps is put at 6,000 men; it comes from Mecklenburg and detachments of it arrive every day'; Beker, as in claim side-a-command for the heading of 30 October; 'I approached the town of Anklam at 8 o'clock in the evening to reconnoitre the bivouac fires set up on the Stettin road; the point I made for was guarded by a picket of hussars supported by infantry; and some peasants, as well as a postillon, who had come out of the town, assured me that it was crowded with fugitives from all the regiments, without being able to answer the questions about the march of General Blücher'; as in claim side-a-command for the fog (OCR); 'he does not know how near the French troops are and does not know besides where to retreat, since I am certain that the Swedes refuse to receive them in Pomerania, except the baggage, which has already been sent into the interior of Pomerania both from Mecklenburg and from Anklam' (OCR); Beker, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading of 31 October; 'I am certain that General Blücher recrossed the Oder 5 days ago with 2 regiments of cavalry and some artillery'; the order, 'order for chef d'escadron Boyer. claims.value: Höpfner: Bila II, needing rest, sent Lieutenant Falkenhausen II of the Bila hussars to Stettin to report to Prince Hohenlohe, and the lieutenant came back with the news that Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau and that the governor of Stettin, negotiating with the enemy, would no longer let General Bila into the fortress and advised him to turn to Swedish Pomerania (OCR passages); Höpfner says the governor's refusal of passage to Bila II brought about the capitulation of Anklam. On the way Bila II learned that the enemy held Ferdinandshof, and the Anklam ferry was found already taken across the Peene; Bila I, who by Höpfner's judgment did very wrong to change direction at once on the statements of men coming back from the Anklam ferry, learned at Leopoldshagen that it was his brother who had reached Uckermünde, that Stettin was invested and that the Swedes had opened the crossing at Pinnow (OCR passages). At Anklam the news of the enemy's approach grew on the morning of the 31st; the parlementaire's demand rested on Stettin's capitulation, for which his brother had fully prepared Bila I.
claims.rationale: From the history of side B: the page images of pp. 217, 225 and 226, with the OCR passages marked. English renderings (ours): 'we left General Bila II' (OCR); 'as rest was necessary, the general sent Lieutenant Falkenhausen II of the Bila hussars to Stettin to report to Prince Hohenlohe, whom he expected there' (OCR); 'the lieutenant soon returned with the news that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau, that the governor of Stettin was in negotiations with the enemy, and had declared to him that he could no longer let General Bila into the fortress, and therefore advised him to turn to Swedish Pomerania' (OCR); 'but the governor saw fit not only to keep back no man for the fortress duty, but even refused General Bila II passage, and thereby brought about the capitulation of Anklam, as will be shown later'; 'but he did learn that the enemy had already occupied Ferdinandshof — on the road from Pasewalk to Anklam' (OCR); 'the Anklam ferry was found already taken away to the Pinnow ferry beyond the Peene' (OCR); 'at Leopoldshagen he stopped, exhausted, and learned that it was his brother who had arrived at Uckermünde, that Stettin was invested and that the Swedes had opened the crossing at Pinnow' (OCR); 'General Bila I had done very wrong in changing direction at once on the statements of those coming back from the Anklam ferry' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the news on the morning of the 31st and for the general's despair; as in claim side-a-command for the parlementaire.

claims.value: Side A sought to cut off the columns making for Stettin: Höpfner has Murat, once Stettin had fallen, arrange to cut them off from the Oder before they learned of its fall, and hurry to Pasewalk, from where Beker's brigade was set moving on Anklam (OCR passages). Murat meant to have Beker summon the corps at Anklam while Lasalle swept the road from Stettin, and meant always to keep Anklam occupied by a detachment (OCR passage); Belliard's instructions were to take the troops met as prisoners of war without written capitulations. After the surrender Murat charged Beker with taking the corps to Spandau with Boussart's brigade and with claiming the treasure, a few leagues from Anklam in the interior of Pomerania, from the authorities of the country, and ordered him to disarm the cavalry but lead its regiments mounted to Potsdam so as to keep 1,400 or 1,500 horses.

claims.value: Side A (French) attacked: Höpfner has Murat hurry to Pasewalk, from where Beker's dragoon brigade was set moving on Anklam (OCR passages), and Murat had Beker summon the corps there, which Beker reported he had done; the French appeared before Anklam as Bila I was leaving it, attacked what remained on the left bank, made as if to cross at Stolpe and sent a parlementaire to summon the general. Side B held the Peene bridge until the parlementaire came, then capitulated.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A advanced on Anklam, attacked and summoned side B, which defended the bridge and capitulated. Tagged inherited: the move on Anklam and the summons were Murat's orders, given before the engagement; the attacks and demonstrations Beker made under them are in claim side-a-command. Friedland, 31 October 1806, 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'I had the honour to announce to you this morning that I was marching on Friedland, and that I would have summoned by General'; 'Beker the enemy corps that was at Anklam, while General Lasalle would push before him everything on the road from Stettin to Anklam, making for Stretense'; 'General Beker reports to me that he has indeed carried out my order, but that he has taken prisoner only the tail of this corps, the rest having crossed the Peene in the night and raised the drawbridge on him. 400 men have fallen into his power, of whom 260 mounted cuirassiers'; Beker, 'General Beker to the Grand Duke of Berg. open_questions: Deferred: the return of the column Beker promised and the return of prisoners by arm and regiment that Belliard asked for (Foucart t. II, p. 596, OCR); a text of the capitulation, if one was written, since Belliard had ordered no more written capitulations; Mathieu Dumas's account, read only as Höpfner quotes it; Murat's letter of the evening of 31 October, to which his letter of 1 November refers, not located; Foucart's footnote on pp. 563-564; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests; Belliard's report to the Major General (Foucart t. II, p. 620, read for the Wolgast entry), whose wagons of flour, grain and baggage taken in the night are taken at a place it does not name and are not assigned to this entry. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the marches, hours and distances of the two Bila columns before Anklam (Höpfner, pp. 220-224), the Prince of Solms-Braunfels's crossing to Usedom (p. 224), Beker's figure in his letter to Lasalle (Foucart t. II, p. 566) and the calibre of the gun Belliard sent (p. 596).

Most consequential gap: side B's strength, and what was taken in the fighting as against at the capitulation. Höpfner's 1100 infantry and 1073 horses, Bodart's 2,200, Beker's count of 1,200 and some mounted cavalry and more than 1,500 infantry, and the 4,000 of the Bulletin and Dumas cannot all describe the same body, and Murat's 400 taken in the tail and Beker's more than 300 cavalry and as many infantry may or may not be inside them. Beker's promised return, or the return Belliard asked for, could settle it.

Disputes kept as separate claims: side B's strength (as above, with the postillon's 6,000, Beker's 2,000 and then 3,000 with 1,000 to 1,200 cavalry, and Murat's 3,000 to 4,000 with 1,400 or 1,500 horses); side B's guns (none, the postillon; guns, Murat; 4 horsed guns, Beker's count; Höpfner names none); the course of the action (Höpfner: a bridge held until a parlementaire came and Hiller's detachments captured outside the town, with no charge; Murat on 31 October: only the tail taken, the rest across the Peene behind a raised drawbridge; Murat on 1 November: a very vigorous charge in the town; the Bulletin and Dumas: a charge on the plain and an entry into the town with the enemy, which Höpfner calls 'so many words, so many untruths'); the French loss (an adjudant sous-officier and a few dragoons, Murat, in a charge that Höpfner's narrative does not have); who commanded side B (General v. Bila, Bodart; the brothers Bila I and Bila II, Höpfner; 2 generals, Beker); names as printed (Becker and Beker; Boussard, Boussart and Broussart).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 1,100 infantry and 1,100 cavalry are Höpfner's 1100 infantry and 1073 horses rounded up, and his 2,200 their sum, by our arithmetic); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Lasalle's, Belliard's, Beker's and Murat's letters and the 25th Bulletin from the page images, with further letters from the OCR; Murat's letters pass on Beker's reports); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history, quoting Mathieu Dumas for the French account; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Anklam passage names no source).
